utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case next on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-94-1-A and 94-1-A bis, the Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you're in communication with us? You're hearing me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May we take the appearances. Mr. Clegg, this is your appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. I appear with Mr. Livingston for the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: A technological failure. I appear with Mr. Livingston for the appellant, Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Upawansa Yapa. I appear for the Prosecution with Mr. Michael Keegan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the Appeals Chamber is hearing the appeal brought by Mr. Tadic. The appeal arises out of a judgement issued by the Chamber on 15 July last year. In that judgement, the Appeals Chamber found the appellant guilty on certain counts on which he had been previously acquitted. The Chamber said, I think with the consent of both sides, that sentencing on those counts would be left for a further procedure. Eventually, after certain steps had been taken, with the consent of both sides, the Appeals Chamber referred the matter for sentencing by a Trial Chamber. That Trial Chamber imposed sentences on the 11th of November. Mr. Tadic now appeals from the sentences imposed. Mr. Clegg is appearing for him. I would just seize the convenience of the moment to itemise what I believe are the principal grounds of appeal to be argued by Mr. Clegg. Telegraphically, the first ground has to do with excessive weight being placed by the Trial Chamber on deterrence as a factor. The second ground has to do with the alleged need to develop a sentencing tariff. The third ground has to do with the question whether Mr. Tadic had made a substantial cooperation with the Prosecution. The fourth ground has to do with the question whether a crime against humanity was intrinsically more serious in law than a war crime. The fifth ground of appeal has to do with the sentencing practice of the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Clegg, have I referred, with the kind of brevity which I foreshadowed, the main grounds of appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Your Honour has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then would it be convenient if we were to stick to that serialisation of the grounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It would, but if I could take them in a slightly different order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please yourself. By all means. Now, the next thing to do under our procedures today, I understand there have been conversations and that in the result the appellant, that's you, Mr. Clegg, would be speaking for 45 minutes. That is your time slot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: No longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No longer. How much time would you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, if I say 45 minutes, I shall take all the credit that is due to me if I finish before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. Then we look forward precisely to your doing that. Then the Prosecutor would take how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Certainly less than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. Then, Mr. Clegg, you would wish to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I would, but I don't anticipate it would be for more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. That errs on the right side of law, because I have you down for 15 minutes. So, Mr. Clegg, would it be convenient for you to take the floor at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It would. I sense that I'm in front of a Tribunal where brevity will never be criticised. The first matter that I would like to re-emphasise to the Court is that obviously what is now effectively a combined appeal, we rely obviously upon the written and oral submissions that were made so far as the appellant's personal circumstances were concerned, the issue as to whether time should be allowed for the period he spent in custody back in Germany and the submissions to be made in relation to the minimum period and other general mitigating factors that were aired when the matter first came before this Trial Chamber. I have no intention, obviously, of repeating those submissions, but I formally adopt them for this hearing. I would like to turn first, if I may, to the question of the desirability of setting out appropriate tariff of sentencing in this Tribunal, and I begin by regretting slightly that I ever used the word "tariff" when I first raised this matter many, many months ago. A better word might have been a "range of sentence," because the word "tariff" does tend to carry with it the implication of a rigid format of sentencing, within narrow brackets. That was never my intention to advance to this Appeals Chamber, the sort of tariff that one finds in the federal courts of the United States of America. That was never my intention. What I intended to submit was that there ought to be a sensible range of sentences passed by the respective Trial Chambers of the International Tribunal, whereby the sentencing, when looked at from one case to another, across the board, gives a broad consistency of approach. It's my basic submission that consistency is consistent with justice and inconsistency breeds a genuine sense of grievance on the part of defendants. It is perhaps very appropriate that today that the judgement was given with two of the Appeals Chamber sitting in the case of Kupreskic. It's my submission that the Trial Chamber in that case perfectly illustrated the desirability of having a range of sentences reflecting the different culpability of individuals who were all charged with what was described in the judgement as being one of the most vicious illustrations of man's inhumanity to man; a description that tragically can be applied to many instances of criminal conduct in the former Yugoslavia over the periods of the conflict. But despite the gravity of the crimes committed in that case, one can see, when one looks, albeit only briefly, as I've only had the opportunity to see it since 9.30 this morning, but when one looks at the respective roles of the people who were convicted before the Trial Chamber in that case, one can see how that is reflected in the ultimate sentences passed by the Court. It's our submission that if you were to compare the role, the seniority, and the crimes of which Dusko Tadic stands convicted today against those that were found in that case, one would see that there was a real substantial disparity. The disparity is most marked when one looks at the position that Tadic held. No one suggests for one moment that he ever had any position of power or influence. He had no position of command. He was not giving orders to others. He was, tragically, in the same position as hundreds, if not thousands of other men in that area of Europe caught up in this conflict, influenced and overtaken by the propaganda to which he had been subjected, and embarking upon a series of criminal acts that, had he not been in the position that he was and subject to the influences that he was, he would never have committed at all. One of the ironies of sentencing in a war crimes tribunal is that one is almost invariably sentencing people who, had they not been caught up with conflict, would have lived their lives without committing any crime at all, and that is also a factor when one turns to consider the value of deterrence. But our primary submission is that the position that Tadic held, his role, his responsibility, his position in the hierarchy, cannot justify a sentence of the length that he now faces, and when compared with the sentences passed earlier today, one can, in our submission, detect a real and serious disparity. The importance is that to have any sense of justice, the sentencing powers of this Tribunal must be exercised equitably, not only between individual people in different cases but against the background of the whole conflict, and it is in this way that the authorities from Nuremberg, after the Second World War, are important. They're important because they are the only yardstick that this Appeals Chamber has to the approach of sentencing in an international forum following a war. The one message that emerges from the Nuremberg sentencing is that those who had positions of power and influence received the highest sentences and that the lower down the hierarchy one came, the lower the sentence became. I won't take the Court through all the cases we have cited in our written submissions, but I know the Court has seen them, has read them, and will reflect on them. But if one considers that in Nuremberg we were considering crimes against humanity that involved participation in the Holocaust, perhaps the most evil crime ever embarked upon by one nation against another race. When we look at the sentences that were passed there, we see that sentences of 25 years would equate to people who had a senior rank in the government or the army. There was, in fact, nobody tried in Nuremberg of an equivalent rank to Dusko Tadic. It's our submission that he had the distinction, of course, of being the first person ever to be tried before the Trial Chamber here in The Hague, and therefore the Trial Chamber did not have the advantage that this Appeals Chamber has today to look at other cases, including the case of Kupreskic decided this morning, in order to try to assess his culpability against that of other people before this Tribunal. But we submit that he has had the sentence pitched far too high to begin with. If we reflect for one moment, if one were to countenance against people who were, in effect, the foot soldiers and who had no command responsibility sentences of 25 years and then seek, in one's mind, to aggregate that sentence up, what, I ask rhetorically, would be the appropriate sentence of somebody who had junior command, local command, national command, and overall strategic command of the war. When one reflects on that, we submit that there is force in the submission that proper and due consideration to an appropriate range of sentence has not been given here. We invite the Appeals Chamber, with respect, to reflect on that. We urge them, those who were not involved in the trial of Kupreskic, to look at that case and to ask oneself rhetorically, if we could pick up the facts of this and put it into that case, what sentence would be passed for somebody with the position and involvement of Dusko Tadic. I remind the Court that in Kupreskic, the crimes there were compared to the very worst death camps in Nazi Germany of Dachau and others, and also the tragedies in Soweto and My Lai. So that is our first simple, short but fundamental submission that a proper application of the range of sentence has not been applied in this case, and understandably so because he was the first ever to be convicted. The matter can be put, perhaps, in just one phrase: We say that there should be comparative culpability and comparative -- comparison, sorry, between the sentences passed in different Trial Chambers. Moving now to the slightly discrete area of whether deterrence is a legitimate part of the approach of the Trial Chamber in sentencing in cases such as this, we would urge the Court to conclude that deterrence so far as people at this level cannot sensibly be assumed to be effective. It is possible that those in command may be deterred by the thought that they will ultimately be brought to justice. But I do ask rhetorically whether it is sensible to envisage that the foot soldiers are capable of being deterred by anything that happens in this Court. I say that, of course, with due deference to the Court, but I reflect for a moment, does anyone believe that had there been a series of trials after the First World War that the camp guards at Dachau or the SS officers in the einzatgruppen would be deterred by that in the Second World War? Is it to be seriously imagined that those involved in the awful massacres in Rwanda would have been deterred by doing so had this Court been able to act more speedily in seeking to bring to justice those involved in these crimes in the area of former Yugoslavia. I venture to suggest that deterrence has a very limited role in sentencing in a domestic criminal jurisdiction. If one looks at all the comparative studies that are done, it by no means indicates that deterrence has any effect in a local criminal jurisdiction. If one looks at Europe, the countries that have the highest crime rate have the highest sentences. Deterrence doesn't seem to work. Ironically, the countries that have the lowest crime rate have lower sentences. If you take that in comparison to the United States, there is no comparative study that indicates that states where the death penalty is passed has a significantly lower death rate than those where there is no death penalty. When one examines the historical and empirical research, there is nothing to indicate that deterrence works on a local level. All the more so on an international level. Before deterrence could ever operate, one would have to ensure that those who were the foot soldiers in some future conflict knew of the sentencing of this Court. In reality, how would that ever be achieved? There can be no deterrence without knowledge. And the very fact that international law tends to reflect crimes committed in conflict that are driven by racial and religious bigotry means that they are much less susceptible to deterrence than crimes motivated out of greed or avarice. We invite the Court to reflect on what has clearly been a conflict of opinion in this arena as to the value of deterrence as a tool of sentencing policy. I remind the Court, of course, of the dissenting judgement of Judge Robinson and also the dissenting judgement of Judge Li. The Court will have seen, in the documents we have submitted, the article by Bing Bing Jai.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, are you still busy with the ground of deterrence or are you moving now to the other ground about the comparison between war crimes and crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am moving now into that ground and I am very grateful for the assistance of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask you one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly to be submitting this: Not that deterrence is not an admissible factor, but that in your submission the Trial Chamber gave too much prominence to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. May I now move, as I already had, to the distinction, if any, between a crime against humanity and a war crime. And I've already alluded, rather earlier than I should, to those two dissenting judgements in the article which I know the Court will have had an opportunity to read already. In our submission, any analysis of sentencing policy ought not to permit there to be a distinction between the penalty passed as a result of the label that the lawyers put on the actions deemed to be criminal. In all domestic jurisdictions that I am aware of, the sentence will normally vary for the same act physically done by a criminal dependent upon his mental state at the time he commits the act. So I think in almost all jurisdictions, a man who kills, intending to kill, will receive an effectively longer sentence than one who kills in an act of passion. The difference is the sentence reflects the culpability of the accused as reflected by his mental state at the time he did the act. Here the distinction is that one is seeking to distinguish in sentence conduct which is, firstly, exactly the same conduct physically, however it is so described, and carries with it exactly the same mental state of mind. The only distinction is the description given to it by the lawyers. In our submission, that is a false premise for distinguishing on sentence. If one reflects for a moment, I think it was the words of the President of the Trial Chamber said punishment should fit the offender. There's an expression in the English criminal law that punishment should fit the crime. Those are words differently describing the sensible jurisprudential object of punishing somebody for what he has done. In our submission, to seek to distinguish between the same conduct done in the same state of mind, differently so described between crimes against humanity and war crimes, goes against that very sensible and fundamental objective. I ask the question which I anticipate, that I know the President asked rhetorically in an earlier judgement: How does one Judge or assess the distinction between the two? What is the yardstick by which to increase or decrease the sentence depending upon verdict? In our submission, there can be no logical or sensible balancing factor to differentiate between those two crimes. It's of course within the knowledge of this Court that the new International Criminal Court will not distinguish between the two offences in, at any rate, the proposal that is currently being considered. Serious war crimes and crimes against humanity. The only assistance that one has before this Tribunal was established is again back in the cases at Nuremberg following the Second World War. And as one can see in the summary of cases set out in our written submissions, no distinction was drawn at Nuremberg between those two crimes, crimes against humanity and war crimes, and it is, we submit, in reality, a distinction with no difference. So I think, finally, on that third ground of appeal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, suppose your friend on the other side were to make this submission, that a second count in respect of what appears to be the same act may be intended to protect a distinct societal interest. Would that be supportive of the kind of distinction against which you are now arguing?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: We would submit not. Any sentencing policy that is intending to protect a society or societorial interest could only do so by deterrence, obviously because one is dealing with the sentencing process after the actual act has occurred. That would tend to imply that if deterrence did work, it would work in a way that distinguished between war crimes and crimes against humanity. So taking the submission to an absurd length, one would have to contemplate a future war criminal in a future conflict saying to himself, "Well, if I do that, that will only be a war crime. So I prefer to do that rather than do something else which may be classified as a crime against humanity, thereby attracting a higher sentence." The absurdity of such a concept, in our submission, illustrates how the idea of seeking to protect a societorial interest, which obviously everybody would seek to do, cannot, in fact, be effective by passing a higher sentence after the event. It can only operate through deterrence and would have to assume an understanding of the distinction which has evaded many lawyers let alone ordinary people. So I think that would be my response. Can I turn very briefly and almost in passing to the last two topics. On reflection, it seemed to Mr. Livingston and I that we had submitted, in relation to the issue of substantial co-operation, already fully before this Appeals Chamber in the last hearing before the appeal -- I'm sorry, the Trial Chamber. May I correct myself. There's been so many hearings before so many different Tribunals in this case. The question of substantial co-operation was fully argued before the Trial Chamber after this Appeal Chamber remitted it for sentencing in relation to the matters that Mr. Tadic had been convicted of following the appeal by the Prosecutor. We rely on those submissions, of which you have a transcript. Having read them, we don't think that there's anything we can usefully add to those. Secondly, so far as the comparative sentencing position of domestic Yugoslav law, that was fully ventilated before this Appeals Chamber in the appeal that was argued at the end of the appeal against conviction, again with one caveat. We don't wish to reargue that but rely on your earlier submissions. The only caveat that we would add is that our analysis of the Yugoslav law would tend to indicate that certainly under local Yugoslav law there is no distinction to be drawn between crimes against humanity and war crimes. And I really pray that in aid on our other head. I'm helpfully reminded by Mr. Livingston that on the question of societorial interest raised by the President of the Appeals Chamber, the dissenting judgement of Judge Robinson, at page 9, deals with a submission that is put far more eloquently than I could have managed, and if I could pray that in aid in response to that rhetorical question that may well have been coming from Mr. Keegan. Unless I can assist the Court any further, those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Clegg. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan will make the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Having in mind Your Honour's comments with respect to the prior sessions and the briefs that have been filed, I will endeavour to keep my remarks limited to the issues raised today by counsel. Beginning first with this question of the creation of sentencing brackets or a range of sentencing perhaps is the term we may now use, we rely primarily upon our submissions already made in our brief, Your Honour, about the impossibility of doing so. It is, of course, an interesting academic question to raise about the possibility of doing so, but that is the essence of the argument; is it possible for this Tribunal or any Tribunal, for that matter, to, in the first instance, proclaim what their considerations with respect to the range of possible sentence will be before they've even considered cases. As we suggest in our submission, this Tribunal is, in fact, in the process of doing that which counsel now argues for, and they are doing so in the appropriate way, on a case-by-case basis. As this is a new endeavour, it will, of course, take time, and one cannot try and bring forward systems that are developed in any particular national jurisdiction which have the benefit of centuries of judicial precedent upon which to draw in saying one can describe what may be the appropriate range of sentences. In the ultimate instance, the range of sentence is set in the Statute, anywhere between no punishment and life imprisonment, and in between that sentences will be determined on a case-by-case basis as they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, Mr. Clegg made the point that this was the first conviction. At the point of time when that conviction was recorded, there would have been no question of there being any range of sentences, but is your friend entitled to take the position that today, in arguing his client's case, he's entitled to refer to such comparative sentences as now exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he would be entitled to do so had that been, in fact, what he did. But that's not, in fact, what he's done. His ground of appeal is that this Appeal Chamber should declare a range of sentences based on apparently some set of objective criteria, and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Didn't he -- I don't reproduce his exact words, but did he not modify that opening argument a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he did. Primarily we would submit, obviously, that having had the benefit of review of our submissions and perhaps of some indications from questions from the Bench in prior hearings. It still raises the ultimate question raised, whether the appellant has satisfied his burden in raising this ground, and that is the focus that we are using in our submissions here, and that is why I say it is important to look at what was the ground of appeal. The original ground of appeal was not: "We want to object to this sentence as being an abuse of discretion by comparing it in detail to the facts and circumstances of other cases before this Tribunal or perhaps the Rwanda Tribunal, in arguing that there is in that comparison proof of an abuse of discretion." The ground of appeal was: "This sentence was unfair because there wasn't some pre-existing sentencing tariff, now range of sentences, by which one could judge what was the sentence if the accused were convicted ahead of time." That, in essence, was the argument.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- the argument. If one were now to follow the argument made today, they still fail on their burden because they have failed to meet the necessary requirements for that burden. There has been no real comparison between the facts and circumstances of this case and of the case, for example, in Kupreskic or indeed of Jelisic, who was sentenced to 40 years for a series of murders, or any other case. Rather, a vague reference that there was a sentence given in a particular case which we submit should draw your attention. Well, in fact, if attention was drawn to that, one could see that in that case there was a sentence given to the accused, the now convicted person Drago Josipovic, for one count of murder under Article 5 of 15 years. That sentence is entirely consistent with the sentences handed down in this case. We'd also note that the sentence to a count of persecution in that case was 25 years. Entirely consistent with the sentence given here. In that instance to the accused Vladimir Santic. Also in this argument, the appellant raises the question of his position, that he had no position in the events which occurred in Prijedor. Well, that in fact is not the case if one details the facts as determined by the Trial Chamber and in fact by the accused's own words in his work report which is part of the record on this appeal, part of the record of the trial, where he claims himself to have been an important person and a voluntary participant in trying to create a greater Serbia; the fact that he was allowed to enter into these camps, commit his various crimes and the murders, that he apparently did hold some sway over members of the military. The Trial Chamber found in the Haskici murders that this accused appeared to be in control of the group of soldiers. So it is not the case that this accused had no position; he had a very real position to his victims and it was, indeed, a position of power. The problem with some sort of criteria is how would one develop it. What ranks would be sufficient? What positions would be sufficient? We submit that it's impossible to do so under the types of crimes and conditions which existed in the conflict that this Tribunal is considering. The appellant would argue that he is nothing more than the same as hundreds, if not thousands of people who were caught up in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Well, that, of course, is not the case at all. There were not hundreds or thousands of people who committed the intentional acts, crimes against humanity and war crimes, that this accused committed. So it is, indeed, a fallacious argument to raise such a defence to his sentence. There were not hundreds or thousands of people who took advantage of the situation, which is what this accused did, to commit crimes for his own benefit or for his own base motives. The appellant also raises the question of the comparison of sentences here to sentences given at the Nuremberg trials. We would submit that that is not entirely a clear and appropriate comparison. The Nuremberg trials, and specifically the trials to which the appellant refers to, was a very specific set of trials which were conducted in a very specific situation; that is, a post-World War II tribunal set up by the allied powers to try those responsible for the crimes committed by the axis powers. The whole issue of how that sentencing was done, of course, was based on the principles considered relevant for sentencing which existed at that time and given that situation, a world war which had gone on for several years. The appellant, of course, does not refer to any of the other trials which were conducted by other tribunals after the Second World War in which many individuals of the same status as this appellant were tried and convicted and, in instances, given more serious sentences than this appellant has received for similar crimes. The last question raised was whether due consideration was given to an appropriate range of punishments in this case. We would submit that the appellant has failed to provide any credible facts or indication from the Trial Chamber's sentencing decision which would indicate that they did not give the appropriate consideration to the full range of sentences, and therefore they have failed to satisfy their burden on this appeal. With respect to the issue of deterrence generally, it would appear that, in fact, the appellant is speaking in what can only be considered contrary positions. The opening statement was that, in fact, deterrence might work for leadership, but is it sensible to envisage that foot soldiers are capable of being deterred. Well, in the very first instance, if, in fact, deterrence does work for the leadership in future situations, there will be no foot soldiers, so we do not even need to raise that issue or get to that question. If we were to follow the logic of the appellant's argument, there would be no reason for this Tribunal to even be here because apparently deterrence is not valid, period, and if deterrence isn't appropriate, then why are we even here? Because that certainly is one of the bases for the establishment and for the purpose of this Tribunal, to not only punish those who perpetrated crimes but to assist in bringing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, Mr. Clegg indicated that he was not taking the position that deterrence was not an admissible factor. So perhaps you might take that into account when framing your submission that deterrence is not to be taken into account at all. I don't think his submissions went as far as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If, in fact, that is the position, although that was not the first part of his argument -- in fact, it appeared to be the contrary, but his final statement in response to your comment was, indeed, that -- if that is the case and the appellant does agree that deterrence is a viable factor, then we stand on our prior submission that they again have failed to provide any facts or clear indication from the judgement of the Trial Chamber that the Trial Chamber gave undue weight. As we submitted in our original brief, they ignored the actual language of that sentencing judgement which indicated that, in fact, deterrence was only one factor considered, and it gives no indication that deterrence was even the main factor. Rather, if there was a main factor, it would appear to be the individual circumstances of this appellant's crimes and circumstances. With respect to the question of crimes against humanity versus war crimes and whether there should be a distinction in terms of sentencing, with respect, it is not the lawyers who label the seriousness of crimes, rather it is a determination by society based on particular interests that it deems necessary to protect that make a distinction between crimes. Mr. Clegg said that, in fact, differences in sentencing are based not on the particular aspects of crime in the sense of how they may be categorised by society but rather on the mental state of the perpetrator and not on a distinction between their labels. Well, in fact, that's not accurate. It is the case in many national jurisdictions that, for example, acts of wilful killing will, indeed, carry different penalties by virtue of the nature of the victim, for example. In many jurisdictions, the murder of a policeman or a public official is deemed to be a more serious act than a wilful killing of another citizen by virtue of the victim's position. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is where the law prescribes a certain differential in the seriousness between crimes. Does the law here prescribe any difference in seriousness between crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The law may prescribe, or may state, in fact, in many jurisdictions, that the position of the victim is an aggravating factor. It is not the case in our jurisdictions that it automatically mandates a more serious sentence. That is the question here. Our submission is that this emphasis on penalty is, in fact, an incomplete analysis of the issue. The fact that in jurisdictions if it is a public official that is murdered does not automatically warrant a more severe sentence, the point is it is considered, all things being equal, a more serious crime than another wilful killing, and that, in essence, we would submit, was the position of the Trial Chamber here following the Erdemovic decision. The language, if we may, was "... all things being equal," a crime against humanity is a more serious offence than an ordinary war crime. That, we believe, is, in fact, an accurate statement of the intent and, if we can say, belief of the International Community at this stage. The references to the question of how were crimes against humanity considered in Nuremberg, we think, again is an incomplete analysis because it completely ignores the development of the international society over the last 50-plus years, and it may be that crimes against humanity being a relatively new invention after the Second World War, that in considering it in the context of that conflict and in those tribunals, the analysis referred to the nature of the acts of the perpetrators which warranted an interpretation of the term "humanity" to mean the nature of the acts, that is, a violation of what would be considered humane behaviour, and not a reference to the fact that the crime in and of itself is violative of humanities, that is, the collective being, the collective society's interest. We would suggest that over the last 50 years that focus has actually changed, and it is, in fact, now the case that the International Community views crimes against humanity as victimising all of society and not just a particular civilian population involved, because such crimes impact on all of us, and the very nature of the International Community's involvement in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, in Rwanda and elsewhere, are evidence of that impact, if you will, of those crimes. So we believe that, in fact, with due respect to Judge Robinson, his citation to the analysis of Dr. Fuad Schwalb in 1946 may not, in fact, be the appropriate analysis at this time, that the vision of crimes against humanity by the International Community has changed and developed and therefore does warrant a determination that, all things being equal, a crime against humanity is a more serious crime than an ordinary war crime. That being said, there is nothing in that statement, nor in that principle that then mandates different punishments as a matter of law. What it does state is that it is within the discretion of a court to say that in a particular case where an accused has been convicted of both, the court believes a more serious sentence should be imposed for the crimes against humanity than the war crimes. It doesn't mean to say that that has to be the situation in every case, nor that it's mandated as a matter of law. I believe one of the examples used by Judge Robinson would be the question of murder, both as a war crime and as a crime against humanity, and that if a sentence to life imprisonment was given for murder as a crime against humanity, it would automatically mandate a lesser sentence for a war crime of murder. Well, we don't believe that that is necessarily the case. It can be, for example, that a war crime in a particular instance may, in fact, be more severe or serious in a given case than a crime against humanity. A war crime which was comprised of a series of murders, for example, of prisoners or other protected persons might, in fact, warrant more severe punishment and be a more serious crime than a crime against humanity of non-violent persecution, where the persecution took the -- the actus reus of the persecution was the denial of fundamental rights of employment or religion, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is that a helpful parallel? Wouldn't you need to focus on the commission of the same act? What Mr. Clegg is saying is that if you bring two different counts charging a crime against humanity and a war crime in respect to the same act, that there should be no difference in penalty. That is how I understand him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But first we must address this issue of whether -- which was his initial point -- there should be no distinction. If it is accepted that there can be a distinction and there should be a distinction in the eyes of the International Community, then we're only dealing with the question of appropriate punishment. Therein lies the question of whether it is within the discretion, the lawful discretion, of a Chamber to say that a particular crime or crimes committed which amount to both violations of Article 5 and Article 2, or Article 3, warrant a more serious punishment for the Article 5 violation than the Article 2 or Article 3, the principle being the Chamber is trying to recognise this distinction, this societal principle, that a crime against humanity is recognised as a more serious crime, all other factors being equal. So in that instance, in fact, we suggest that with all the other principles recognised, that is a lawful exercise of discretion and this appellant has failed to address that particular aspect and has failed to satisfy his burden that there was an abuse by this Trial Chamber in its determination. Unless we can assist you any further, Your Honour, those would be our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just to compare notes. I understand you to be saying that whatever was the position in 1945, there has since then been a progression in the evolution of customary international law so that today a crime against humanity is seen as being directed to a societal interest which is distinct from the societal interests to which a war crime is directed, and that accordingly, the penalty for the former should be greater than the penalty for the latter in the normal case, all things being equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would just qualify that by saying that a distinction in penalty is not an abuse of discretion by a court given the state of international law at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Then, Mr. Clegg, would it be convenient for you to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Our slot says 15 minutes, but you were good enough to indicate a lesser period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I will try to be good to my word. Can I just remind the Court that we never sought to ask you to declare a tariff of sentencing like the Supreme Court -- like the Federal Court in America has. What we asked you to do was to develop, have regard to the need to develop a tariff. In other words, it is an ongoing process. And there is, we submit, a very important distinction between those two propositions. We never said that you should, as it were, declare some rigid list of sentences to be applied irrespective of the justice of the case across the board to people charged before this Tribunal. Too rigid an adherence to a tariff can result in as much injustice as having no regard to comparative sentencing at all. All we're seeking to say is there ought to be a broad comparison between the sentences passed in different cases, and, therefore, we say that this Appeal Chamber now has an advantage that the Trial Chamber did not have in being able to look at comparative sentences which they could not do because there was nothing to compare it with since 1945. That advantage, which you have and they didn't, allows one to look at comparable cases, and I rely particularly on the one today, in order to reflect upon whether the sentencing here has been pitched too high. There is nothing wrong in that approach. We would submit it's the perfectly sensible approach for this Appeal Chamber to adopt, and to do anything else would leave an appellant with a sense of injustice. If this Appeal Chamber were to say, "We close our eyes to what other Trial Chambers have done by way of sentencing and will not look at it," it would be, we suggest, an absurd consequence of this process. I'm not sure upon what material the respondent relies to say there are not hundreds or thousands of people in the former Yugoslavia who would have committed war crimes. I invite the Court just to reflect on the historical events in that region. The Court may well conclude from the number of camps and inevitably the number of people that must have been employed to work in the camps, the collection of people, and the awful genocide that occurred, that there must, indeed, have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people who were involved in one degree or another in these crimes. It's perhaps not possible to give any quantified number to them at this stage in history. But if one goes back to the Second World War, it is undoubtedly the case that tens of thousands of perfectly ordinary citizens were involved in putting into effect the Nazi policy called "The Final Solution" by which Hitler determined that all the Jews of Europe should be killed. It is a sad and remarkable historical fact that in times of war, ordinary people will become embroiled in activity that they would never have countenanced at any other time in their life. We do rely upon the Second World War cases because there is nothing else. There's been nothing since that until now. And the respondents say that there has been a development of customary international law, and I'm now dealing with the distinction to be drawn in sentence between war crimes and crimes against humanity, but without relying upon any case, decision, article, book published between 1945 and the beginning of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia in order to identify such a development. In our submission, there is nothing to indicate that societorial interests in 1945 were any less in protecting or seeking to protect the Jews of Europe than the societorial interests of the Muslims of the former Yugoslavia. And we don't accept, with respect, the proposition that the societorial interests of the Jews at the end of the Second World War were somehow abrogated in way they would not have been now. The whole thrust of Nuremberg was to seek to effect just reparation for what had happened to those people. Unless I could assist the Appeal Chamber any further, those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're obliged to counsel. We appreciate the assistance we have had from both sides. This has been a relatively brief presentation, and it would be appropriate if the decision were to follow speedily. I think we should be in a position to give you a decision fairly quickly, but I will not now announce the date. We will go into consultations and we will alert you to that eventuality in due course. For the moment, therefore, we would retire. The Appeals Chamber will retire to consider its decision. Unless there is any other matter which demands attention, the Appeals Chamber will, therefore, stand adjourned.
